extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for making and supporting obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 (and pre‑AIA equivalents), including how to determine prior art scope, differences to claimed subject matter, level of ordinary skill, acceptable rationales, search scope, and how to treat applicant replies and rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) must be applied for references that are U.S. patents or publications with earlier filing dates when the statutory conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply form paragraph 7.12.fti (AIPA and later amendments) when the reference is a U.S. patent or a publication of a U.S. application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a), or a U.S. patent issued from or a publication of an international application with an international filing date on/after Nov. 29, 2000, or a U.S. patent issued from an international design application that designates the United States. See Examiner Notes for determination of pre‑AIA 102(e) date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑AIPA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (international applications filed before Nov. 29, 2000)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre‑AIPA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (form paragraph 7.12.01.fti) applies where the reference is a U.S. patent issued directly or indirectly from an international application filed prior to November 29, 2000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.12.01.fti and consult Examiner Notes to determine the correct pre‑AIPA 102(e) date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit claims and effective filing date determination
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining a pre‑AIA 102(e) date, consider benefit claims to earlier‑filed U.S. provisional, nonprovisional, and international applications under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, 365(c), and 386(c) only if the subject matter used to make the rejection is appropriately supported in the earlier application's disclosure (and any intermediate applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A benefit claim to a U.S. patent issuing from an earlier‑filed international application (with international filing date prior to Nov. 29, 2000) may only result in an effective U.S. filing date as of the date the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 371(c)(1),(2) and (4) were fulfilled. Do NOT consider benefit claims to U.S. applications filed before an international application that has an international filing date prior to Nov. 29, 2000. Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)‑(d), 365(a) or (b), or 386(a) or (b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional application support requirement for benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference (U.S. patent, published U.S. patent application, or WIPO publication) is entitled to the benefit of the filing date of a provisional application only if at least one of the claims in the reference is supported by the written description of the provisional application in compliance with pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph or 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Dynamic Drinkware v. National Graphics and Amgen v. Sanofi for case law on provisional support; ensure claim support in the provisional before attributing its filing date to the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of international application publications with pre‑Nov. 29, 2000 filing dates
rubrics_metrics.description: If a PCT publication (including voluntary U.S. publication under 35 U.S.C. 122 of the national stage or a WIPO PCT publication) has an international filing date prior to Nov. 29, 2000, did not designate the United States, or was not published in English by WIPO, it is not a prior art reference under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use form paragraph for 102(e) in this situation; the reference may be applied under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (b) as of its publication date (see form paragraphs 7.08.fti and 7.09.fti).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs and paragraph precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain rejections must be preceded by specific form paragraphs before applying a 102(e) rejection paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ¶7.15.02.fti/7.15.03.fti must be preceded by 7.12.fti or 7.12.01.fti; patent application publications may only be used if preceded by 7.12.fti; for applications with filing date on/after Mar.16,2013 claiming priority/benefit to pre‑Mar.16,2013 filings, paragraph 7.06 must precede. Insert appropriate wording in brackets per instructions (e.g., --assignee--, --applicant--, or --joint inventor--).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 101 and double patenting / priority issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. 101, two patents cannot issue on identical subject matter; claims directed to the same invention claimed in the reference should be rejected (or provisionally rejected) and applicant should be required to resolve any issue of priority and possible nonstatutory double patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraphs 8.30‑8.32 for identity rejections, form paragraph 8.27.fti for priority issues, and form paragraph 8.33 (with at least one of 8.34‑8.39) for nonstatutory double patenting. See MPEP §804 subsection II.A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection for public use or on sale (pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) based upon a public use or sale of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 7.16.fti must be preceded by form paragraphs 7.07.fti and 7.09.fti or 7.103. A full explanation of the evidence establishing a public use or sale must be provided in the Office action (insert in bracket 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection for abandonment of invention (pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c) if the invention has been abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 7.17.fti must be preceded by 7.07.fti and 7.10.fti or 7.103. Provide a full explanation of the evidence establishing abandonment in the Office action (see MPEP §2134).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection for foreign patenting (pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) as barred by applicants' foreign patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 7.18.fti must be preceded by 7.07.fti and 7.11.fti or 7.103. The Office action must include appropriate dates and explain how they make the foreign patent available as prior art under 102(d). Refer to MPEP §2135.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection for applicant not being the inventor (pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) where the applicant did not invent the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 7.19.fti must be preceded by paragraphs 7.07.fti and 7.13.fti or 7.103. Insert explanation of supporting evidence establishing that the applicant was not the inventor (see MPEP §2137).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory standard for obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may not be obtained if differences between the claimed invention and prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made. This applies to FITF/AIA applications using the effective filing date in place of time of invention; see MPEP §2150 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR decision and flexible approach to obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR v. Teleflex endorses a flexible approach to obviousness, warns against rigid TSM application, and emphasizes common sense and predictable results when combining familiar elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR identified errors in overly narrow TSM application and emphasized that combinations yielding predictable results are likely obvious. Use common sense but support invoked common sense with evidence and reasoned explanation (see Arendi v. Apple). Rejections must be consistent with Graham framework and the Supreme Court precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries to resolve obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is a legal conclusion based on underlying factual inquiries: (A) scope and content of the prior art; (B) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (C) level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include objective evidence (secondary considerations) such as commercial success, long‑felt need, failure of others, unexpected results when present; weight is case‑by‑case. These factors control any obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining scope and content of the prior art (search guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain a thorough understanding of the invention by reading specification and claims (give claims the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification). The search should cover claimed subject matter and disclosed features reasonably expected to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow general search guidelines in MPEP §904‑§904.03. Prior art may be in the applicant's field or reasonably pertinent (analogous art). Searches should prefer references that provide teaching/suggestion/motivation to combine if such exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertaining differences between claim and prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret claim language and consider both the invention and prior art as a whole to ascertain differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2111 for claim interpretation and MPEP §2141.02 for considering invention and prior art as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness rejection should include, explicitly or implicitly, an indication of the level of ordinary skill in view of the prior art applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider: (1) type of problems encountered; (2) prior art solutions; (3) rapidity of innovations; (4) sophistication of technology; (5) educational level of active workers. Use these to determine what a person of ordinary skill would have known, could do, and be expected to do. Office personnel may rely on their technical expertise and are presumed to have relevant competence (see In re Berg, PowerOasis v. T‑Mobile).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to articulate factual findings and rationale for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must articulate findings of fact concerning state of the art and teachings of references and must provide explanation(s) supporting an obviousness rejection; conclusory statements are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 132 requires notice of the reasons for rejection. Rejections must include a reasoned explanation with rational underpinning (quoting In re Kahn). Failure to articulate findings may lead to appeal, and examiners must include explicit findings when necessary (e.g., how a POSITA would have understood prior art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptable lines of reasoning to support obviousness include combining known elements to yield predictable results, simple substitution, applying known techniques to improve similar devices, applying known techniques to devices ready for improvement, 'obvious to try' when a finite number of predictable solutions exist with reasonable expectation of success, known work prompting predictable variations across fields, and some teaching/suggestion/motivation in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed rationales (A‑G) in the MPEP are illustrative but not exhaustive. See MPEP §2143 and §2144‑§2144.09 for examples and further guidance. Even when invoking TSM, avoid rigid application and ensure articulated reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's reply requirements under 37 C.F.R. 1.111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the Office has established Graham factual findings and concluded obviousness, the burden shifts to the applicant to show the Office erred in the findings or to provide evidence showing nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must distinctly and specifically point out alleged errors in the Office action per 37 C.F.R. 1.111(b). An effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the Office erred; mere assertions that a prima facie case was not established or unsupported reliance on common knowledge are not substantively adequate and may result in repetition of the rejection and a final action (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence and secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must consider all timely rebuttal evidence, including secondary considerations such as commercial success, long‑felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results, when reevaluating an obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may submit evidence to rebut factual findings; Office personnel should articulate factual findings that support the rationale relied upon. Examples of rebuttal arguments include demonstrating technological difficulties that would have prevented one of ordinary skill from combining claimed elements by known methods.
